title: Counting
intro: With equally likely outcomes, probability is counting. A few principles (multiply choices, divide out orderings that do not matter) handle almost every case.

blocks.text: If a task is done in stages with $n_1$ choices at the first, $n_2$ at the second and so on (whatever was chosen before), there are $n_1n_2\cdots$ ways in all. Everything below is this principle plus division by overcounting.

items: Ordered selections of $k$ from $n$ without repetition: $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1) = \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}$.
Unordered selections: each unordered set appears $k!$ times among the ordered ones, so divide: $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$.
Arrangements of a word with repeated letters: $\frac{n!}{n_1!n_2!\cdots}$, the multinomial coefficient.
With repetition allowed, $k$ ordered draws from $n$: $n^k$.

blocks.text: The number of ways to put $k$ identical balls into $n$ distinguishable boxes is $\binom{n+k-1}{k}$: line up $k$ stars and $n-1$ bars and choose where the bars go. The same count gives the number of non-negative integer solutions of $x_1 + \cdots + x_n = k$. Note that these arrangements are not equally likely if the balls are thrown at random, a classic trap.

Among $n$ people with birthdays independent and uniform over 365 days, the chance that all are different is $\frac{365}{365}\cdot\frac{364}{365}\cdots\frac{365-n+1}{365}$. Since there are $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs, each matching with probability $1/365$, collisions arrive much sooner than intuition suggests: roughly when $n^2/730\approx\ln 2$, that is $n\approx23$. The same square-root effect sets the strength of hash functions against collision attacks.

blocks.source:
from math import comb, perm, prod
import numpy as np
deck = comb(52, 5)
full_house = 13 * comb(4, 3) * 12 * comb(4, 2)
flush = 4 * comb(13, 5) - 40                        # remove straight flushes (incl. royal)
print(f"5-card hands: {deck:,}")
print(f"full house: {full_house:,}  P = {full_house / deck:.6f}")
print(f"flush (not straight flush): {flush:,}  P = {flush / deck:.6f}")
# Birthday problem: P(some shared birthday among n people), 365 equally likely days
def p_shared(n): return 1 - prod((365 - k) / 365 for k in range(n))
for n in (10, 23, 40, 70):
    print(f"n = {n}: P(shared birthday) = {p_shared(n):.4f}")
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
sim = np.mean([len(set(rng.integers(0, 365, 23))) < 23 for _ in range(50000)])
print(f"simulated, n = 23: {sim:.4f}")
print("ordered vs unordered: P(10, 3) =", perm(10, 3), " C(10, 3) =", comb(10, 3))

blocks.text: Output of the run: there are 2 598 960 five-card hands; 3 744 are full houses (probability 0.00144) and 5 108 are flushes that are not straight flushes (0.00197). The probability of a shared birthday is 0.117 for 10 people, 0.507 for 23, 0.891 for 40 and 0.9992 for 70; a simulation for 23 gives 0.509.

blocks.title: Mississippi
blocks.text: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of MISSISSIPPI are there?
solution: 11 letters: M once, I four times, S four times, P twice.

blocks.title: Two pair
blocks.text: Find the probability that a five-card poker hand is two pair.
solution: Choose the two ranks for the pairs: $\binom{13}{2} = 78$; the suits of each pair: $\binom42^2 = 36$; the fifth card from the other 11 ranks: 44.

blocks.title: Stars and bars
blocks.text: In how many ways can 10 identical sweets be shared among 4 children (some may get none)? And if each must get at least one?
solution: Give each child one first, then share the remaining 6 freely: $\binom{6 + 3}{3} = 84$.
